title: {{NAME}} and the Roar That Shook the Mountain
moral: True strength is knowing when to be gentle.

pages.content: The distress call reached {{NAME}} through the amber crystal that lived in the pocket of his jade suit, a warm vibration that preceded the thin, urgent voice of Thorn, the eldest of the Mountain Fairies. {{NAME}} was at the base of the Ironback Range within twenty minutes, the kind of mountain range that looked as if the earth had simply lost its patience and shoved upward. The problem was visible from a long way off: a landslide, or what had been a landslide before it had been caught and held in place by the most extraordinary thing {{NAME}} had ever seen. A Brachiosaurus, easily thirty metres from feet to head, was standing at the mountain's foot with both her enormous front legs braced against the sliding rock face, her neck curved low with effort, and she was holding the whole mass of rubble in place with her body, because behind the rock face, barely visible through the gaps between boulders, was the entrance to the Mountain Fairy colony. The Brachiosaurus had been holding on for four hours. Her name, Thorn told him, was Mira.

pages.content: Thorn was a fairy of considerable age and no patience for anything she considered a waste of time, which was most things. She manifested before {{NAME}} as a concentrated point of amber light the size of a large moth, and delivered her briefing in rapid, precise sentences like a general with three minutes to spare. 'The colony is one hundred and forty-three fairies, twelve of them children, three of them elderly and non-mobile. The entrance tunnel is blocked at two points. Mira can hold for perhaps another two hours before her muscles fail. You are the fastest moving object I have access to. There are two objectives: clear the tunnel and shore up the rock face so Mira can step back.' She paused. 'Can you do this?' {{NAME}} looked at the Brachiosaurus. Mira's eyes found him, vast and deep as tide pools, full of a trust so enormous it was almost its own kind of weight. He wanted very badly to say yes with complete confidence. 'I can do the first part,' he said honestly. 'For the second part I need your fairies.' Thorn considered this for exactly half a second. 'Acceptable,' she said.

pages.content: {{NAME}} moved fast, the way he always moved in situations that did not allow for hesitation, with a certainty borrowed from the task itself rather than from himself. The first tunnel blockage was a single vast boulder wedged across the entrance. He braced, found the fulcrum point the way his physics knowledge told him to, and shifted it aside with a controlled explosion of force that sent rock dust billowing. The second blockage was worse, a mesh of smaller stones interlocked like a bad puzzle, the kind where removing one piece wrong would collapse the others onto the fairy children behind them. He stopped. He breathed. He picked out the keystone with his fingertips, gentle as if defusing something precious, and removed stones one by one in an order that was essentially a conversation with gravity. The fairies emerged in single file behind Thorn, the elderly carried by the young, the fairy children wide-eyed and dusty but unharmed. When the last one stepped into the mountain air, Thorn landed on {{NAME}}'s knuckle and said nothing for a moment, which from Thorn was extraordinary.

pages.content: For the rock face, Thorn's plan was extraordinary. She called every fairy to the surface. One hundred and forty-three of them, from the eldest to the smallest child, arrayed themselves across the unstable rock in a pattern only Thorn could see, each one pressing both hands against the stone and humming, a deep collective sound that was nothing like the tiny voices they usually carried. The rock face shivered. Then it stilled. The fairies were not moving the rocks. They were speaking to them, in the old language of stone that the Mountain Fairies alone remembered, persuading the rockfall to find its own stable configuration. The sound they made was ancient and powerful and unbearably beautiful, and Mira heard it. The great Brachiosaurus lifted her head slowly, testing, then stepped back with the terrible carefulness of something massive that is trying not to disturb the air. The rock face held. It held, and held, and the last stone settled with a sound like a deep sigh, and held still. Mira turned her vast head toward the fairies and made a sound deep in her chest like a bell inside a mountain. Every fairy sat down where they stood, utterly spent.

pages.content: The fairy children, who had recovered more quickly than the elders with the extraordinary resilience of the very young, immediately climbed {{NAME}}'s cape and sat in a row along his shoulders, chattering in voices like a handful of tiny bells thrown in the air. He stood beside Mira in the evening light, the great dinosaur resting her neck along the ground, her breathing finally slow and even. Her eyes were half-closed. {{NAME}} sat beside her head, which was roughly the size of his bedroom, and put his hand against the warm, rough scales of her cheek. She made that deep bell-sound again, very quietly. Thorn landed on {{NAME}}'s knee, looking, for the first time, something other than brisk. 'She was alone when it started,' Thorn said. 'She simply did not leave.' {{NAME}} thought about that for a long time. The fairy children on his shoulders had started braiding small flowers into his cape's amber inner lining with great creativity and without asking permission. He decided not to mention it. He fell asleep sitting up, and dreamed of something immovable and warm, and in the morning the flowers were still there, and so was Mira, still sleeping.
